title: Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett's holding company, enters the game
what: Berkshire Hathaway of Omaha began as a New England textile maker and now owns insurance companies, See's Candies, the Buffalo Evening News and 60% of Blue Chip Stamps, and invests its insurers' money in shares. In his annual letter of 3 March, chairman Warren Buffett reports book value of 335.85 dollars per share at the end of 1979, with shares held by the insurers counted at market value, up from 19.46 dollars when he took control in the mid-1960s. Berkshire pays no dividend and has never split its share, so one share costs a few hundred dollars.
why: Listing beat: Yahoo's history starts in March 1980, and the game lists the share in May, a quiet month. From here to today a single share rises from 260 to about 750,000 dollars, the steadiest compounder of the game.

title: Buffett: book value up to 400.80 dollars, a third of GEICO
what: In his letter dated 27 February Buffett reports book value per share of 400.80 dollars at the end of 1980, a compound gain of 20.5% a year since present management took over sixteen years ago. Berkshire's insurers now own 7.2 million shares of the car insurer GEICO. The textile business lost money in 1980.
why: The yearly letter is the main news a Berkshire shareholder gets; GEICO became the crown jewel, bought fully in 1995-96.

title: Berkshire's net worth rose 40% in 1982
what: Buffett's letter of 3 March reports that Berkshire's net worth rose 208 million dollars, or 40%, in 1982, to 737.43 dollars per share, a compound 22% a year over 18 years. He warns the percentage will diminish as Berkshire grows. The stock market has been rising since last August.
why: The 1982-83 bull market and Berkshire's own gains drove the best twelve months of the arc (+125% from 1982-09 to 1983-09).

title: Berkshire buys Nebraska Furniture Mart
what: Berkshire has bought most of Nebraska Furniture Mart in Omaha, the furniture store built by Rose Blumkin, for about 60 million dollars. Earlier this year Berkshire merged with Blue Chip Stamps, in which it held 60%, and now owns it entirely.
why: A classic Buffett purchase of an owner-run business. The exact month of the deal is not confirmed by the sources read; Berkshire's letter counts its earnings from the fourth quarter.

title: Buffett backs Capital Cities' purchase of ABC
what: On 18 March Berkshire agreed to buy three million new shares of Capital Cities Communications at 172.50 dollars each, about 517 million dollars, to help it buy the ABC television network for 3.5 billion dollars. ABC is about four times the size of Capital Cities.
why: Explains the +22% month (market flat): the deal showed Berkshire as a force in big-company finance. The stake later turned into a large Disney holding in 1996.

title: Berkshire's net worth jumped 48% in 1985
what: Buffett's letter of 4 March reports that net worth rose 613.6 million dollars, or 48.2%, in 1985, to 1,643.71 dollars a share. Right after year end Berkshire bought Scott Fetzer of Cleveland, maker of World Book encyclopedias and Kirby vacuum cleaners, for about 320 million dollars, and its Capital Cities/ABC stake is now in place. 'Neither will be seen again in my lifetime,' Buffett says of Halley's Comet and the percentage gain.
why: Berkshire's share price nearly doubled in 1985; the letter confirms the business behind it.

title: Buffett puts 700 million dollars into Salomon
what: Berkshire agreed to buy 700 million dollars of Salomon Inc preferred stock paying 9% and convertible into common stock at 38 dollars a share. Salomon uses the money to buy back shares from its largest holder, Minorco, which the raider Ronald Perelman had sought to acquire. Berkshire gets two seats on Salomon's board.
why: Berkshire's largest investment yet; it later pulled Buffett into running Salomon during its 1991 scandal.

title: Buffett reveals a 600 million dollar bet on Coca-Cola
what: Berkshire's annual letter, dated 28 February, shows that in 1988 it bought 14,172,500 shares of Coca-Cola for 592.5 million dollars, worth 632.4 million at year end, and the maximum allowed stake in Freddie Mac. Buffett says Berkshire intends to hold such stocks for a long time. Net worth rose 20% in 1988.
why: The most famous Buffett holding, and the start of the 1989 rally in Berkshire's shares (+85% that year). The letter's exact publication date is not confirmed; see Unexplained moves for the +27% in April.

title: Berkshire jumps 27% to 6,275 dollars a share around its annual meeting
what: Berkshire Hathaway shares rose 27% in April to 6,275 dollars, against a market up 5%. Shareholders gathered in Omaha on 24 April for the annual meeting, the first since the share moved to the New York Stock Exchange in November and since Warren Buffett disclosed in his February letter that Berkshire had put 593 million dollars into Coca-Cola, which is already worth more. Berkshire pays no dividend and has never split its share; a round lot of 100 shares now costs more than 600,000 dollars.
why: No single cause found: the letter (28 February 1989), the meeting date and the NYSE listing are sourced; that the April jump followed from the meeting and the Coca-Cola news is inferred, the share was thinly traded. Curator asked about this month.
source: https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1988.html (read 2026-10-03); price changes from data/out/brk.json and data/reference/sp500.json

title: Berkshire invests 600 million dollars in Gillette
what: On 21 July Berkshire agreed to invest 600 million dollars in Gillette through securities paying 8.75% that can be turned into about 11% of Gillette's shares after two years. Buffett called Gillette 'exactly the sort of business in which we like to invest for the long term'. Analysts see it as protection against hostile bidders.
why: Another of the 'white squire' deals of the late 1980s (Salomon, Gillette, USAir, Champion).

title: A weak 1990, and a big bet on Wells Fargo
what: Buffett's letter of 1 March reports net worth up only 7.3% in 1990, after a fall for much of the second half. Berkshire bought nearly 10% of the bank Wells Fargo for 290 million dollars, less than five times earnings, while bank stocks were in a panic.
why: Berkshire's share price fell about 23% in 1990; the Wells Fargo purchase is a textbook example of buying fear.

title: Buffett takes charge of scandal-hit Salomon
what: After Salomon Brothers admitted that a trader had submitted false bids in US Treasury auctions, Warren Buffett was elected interim chairman of Salomon Inc on 18 August. Berkshire's 700 million dollar investment in Salomon is at stake, and Buffett has promised to clean up the firm.
why: Buffett's reputation on the line; he ran Salomon for ten months and saved it. Berkshire's investment survived.

title: Berkshire's book value up 20% in 1992; Buffett back from Salomon
what: Buffett's letter of 1 March reports that book value per share rose 20.3% in 1992, to 7,745 dollars, a compound 23.6% a year over 28 years. Last June Buffett stepped down as interim chairman of Salomon Inc after ten months; Salomon Brothers has since reported record pre-tax earnings.
why: Steady compounding through the early 1990s; the share price rose about 30% in 1992 and 39% in 1993.

title: Berkshire to buy all of GEICO; Cap Cities stake becomes Disney
what: On 25 August Berkshire agreed to buy the half of the car insurer GEICO it does not already own, for about 2.3 billion dollars. Last month Disney agreed to buy Capital Cities/ABC, in which Berkshire is the largest shareholder; Berkshire will exchange its stake for Disney shares and cash.
why: GEICO became the core of Berkshire's insurance float; the Disney stake linked the two arcs.

title: Berkshire sells a cheaper Class B share
what: In May Berkshire sold new Class B shares, each worth 1/30 of the existing share, which is now called Class A. It sold 517,500 of them, raising 565 million dollars, in response to plans by others to market unit trusts as Berkshire look-alikes.
why: The A share in the game is unchanged; the B share widened Berkshire's ownership. Details are from the 1996 letter (published in 1997); the May 1996 prospectus was listed but not read.

title: Berkshire to buy General Re for 22 billion dollars in stock
what: On 19 June Berkshire agreed to buy the reinsurer General Re in exchange for Berkshire shares, a deal worth about 22 billion dollars and Berkshire's biggest ever. Buffett and Charlie Munger have agreed to vote their shares in favour.
why: Doubled Berkshire's insurance float, but Buffett later called paying in stock a mistake: Gen Re's underwriting losses (and 9/11) hurt, and Berkshire's share price peaked in 1998 and fell for over a year.

title: Buffett's worst year, then the tech bubble bursts
what: Buffett's letter of 1 March calls 1999 Berkshire's worst year under his management: book value rose just 0.5%, the worst result of his tenure both in absolute terms and compared with the S&P 500. Berkshire will buy back its shares only when they sell well below their value, he writes. On 10 March, the day the Nasdaq index peaked at 5,132, Berkshire's shares traded at 40,800 dollars, their lowest since mid-1997; since then technology shares have tumbled and Berkshire's have risen sharply.
why: Explains the +30% month (market +10%): the rotation out of technology into 'old economy' stocks. Buffett's refusal to buy tech looked foolish in 1999 and right from here on.

title: September 11 brings the biggest insurance loss ever
what: The attacks of 11 September have caused the largest insured loss in history, estimated at around 40 billion dollars for the industry. Berkshire, through General Re and its other reinsurers, is expected to be among the largest payers, with losses of more than 2 billion dollars. Stock exchanges were closed until 17 September.
why: Buffett admitted in his next letter that he had let General Re take on risks without safeguards. Book value fell 6.2% in 2001.

title: Berkshire buys Wal-Mart's distribution arm McLane
what: Berkshire agreed in May to buy McLane Company, the grocery distributor, from Wal-Mart. Berkshire keeps buying whole companies for cash: Shaw carpets, Johns Manville and Fruit of the Loom in the last two years.
why: The years when Berkshire became a conglomerate of whole businesses rather than mainly a portfolio; the share price moved little from 1998 to 2003.

title: Investigators close in on General Re
what: On 20 May Berkshire said its General Re unit had ended the consulting contract of its former chief executive Ronald Ferguson, after he invoked the Fifth Amendment when questioned by the SEC and the Justice Department in their investigations.
why: The investigations concerned a General Re deal with the insurer AIG (not named in the release); they ended in 2010 settlements, recorded in a Berkshire filing of January 2010.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1067983/000095012905005674/v09493e8vk.htm (Berkshire press release of 20 May 2005, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1067983/000119312510008916/d8k.htm (Berkshire 8-K of January 2010, read 2026-10-03)

title: Buffett to give most of his fortune to the Gates Foundation
what: Warren Buffett announced in June that he will give away 85% of his Berkshire shares to five foundations in yearly gifts starting in July, the largest share going to the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. It is the largest charitable pledge in history.
why: Settles what happens to Buffett's controlling stake: it will be sold or given away gradually, not dumped at once.

title: In the panic, Buffett invests in Goldman Sachs
what: On 23 September, in the middle of the financial panic, Berkshire bought perpetual preferred stock in Goldman Sachs paying a 10% dividend. Buffett's money is read as a vote of confidence in the battered investment bank.
why: Berkshire as a lender of last resort in 2008. Berkshire's shares held up in September (+12%) but fell 44% from end-2007 to February 2009. The size of the investment (commonly reported as 5 billion dollars) was not confirmed in the sources read.

title: Buffett: 2008 was our worst year, and I did dumb things
what: In his letter of 27 February Buffett reports that book value per share fell 9.6% in 2008, the worst year in 44 years both for Berkshire and for the S&P 500. He admits he did 'some dumb things in investments', among them buying ConocoPhillips shares near the peak of oil prices. Berkshire's shares have fallen with the market.
why: The bottom of the arc's worst stretch (-44% from 2007-12 to 2009-02). The letter says he bought ConocoPhillips 'when oil and gas prices were near their peak'.

title: Berkshire buys the BNSF railway: 'an all-in bet on America'
what: On 3 November Berkshire offered 26 billion dollars in cash and shares for the 77% of Burlington Northern Santa Fe it does not already own, valuing the railway at about 44 billion dollars including debt. It is the largest acquisition in Berkshire's history. To let small BNSF holders take Berkshire stock, Berkshire will split its B shares 50 for 1; the A share is not split.
why: The turn towards capital-heavy businesses (railway, utilities) that defines today's Berkshire. The deal closed in February 2010.

title: Berkshire to buy Lubrizol for 9.7 billion dollars
what: On 14 March Berkshire agreed to buy the chemicals company Lubrizol for 135 dollars a share in cash, a 28% premium, in a deal valued at about 9.7 billion dollars including debt, one of the largest in Berkshire's history.
why: Buffett's first big deal after BNSF, part of the steady build-up of whole businesses.

title: Berkshire and 3G to buy Heinz for 28 billion dollars
what: On 14 February Heinz agreed to be bought by Berkshire Hathaway and the Brazilian investment firm 3G Capital for 72.50 dollars a share in cash, a 20% premium, in a deal valued at 28 billion dollars including debt. It is the largest deal ever in the food industry.
why: Heinz, later merged with Kraft, became one of Buffett's disappointments; at the time it showed Berkshire's appetite for very large deals.

title: Berkshire's biggest industrial deal: Precision Castparts
what: On 8 August Berkshire agreed to buy Precision Castparts, maker of metal parts for jet engines, for 235 dollars a share in cash, a deal of about 37 billion dollars including debt.
why: Buffett later wrote down its value by about 10 billion dollars, admitting he overpaid.

title: Berkshire buys Apple shares
what: Berkshire disclosed that it began buying Apple shares in the first three months of the year, a rare investment in a technology company for a firm whose chairman has long avoided them.
why: Apple became Berkshire's largest holding and its best investment of the era. The disclosure month (quarterly filing in May) is not confirmed by the sources read; Wikipedia says Berkshire began investing in the first quarter of 2016.

title: Berkshire loosens its rules for buying back its own shares
what: On 17 July Berkshire's board scrapped the rule that it may buy back shares only at no more than 20% above book value. Now repurchases can be made whenever Buffett and Munger believe the price is below Berkshire's intrinsic value, as long as cash stays above 20 billion dollars.
why: Opened the way to large buybacks, a new support for the share price.

title: Berkshire buys into Japan's five big trading houses
what: On 31 August Berkshire said it had bought slightly more than 5% of each of Japan's five leading trading companies, Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo, over about twelve months. It intends to hold them for the long term and may go up to 9.9% in each.
why: A rare big foreign bet that paid off handsomely; it came after a pandemic year in which Berkshire had found little to buy.

title: Berkshire completes the purchase of Alleghany
what: Berkshire completed its purchase of the insurer Alleghany for about 11.6 billion dollars in October.
why: Berkshire held up in the 2022 bear market: its shares rose about 4% in the year while the market fell. The exact closing date in October was not checked.

title: Charlie Munger dies at 99
what: Charlie Munger, Berkshire's vice chairman since 1978 and Warren Buffett's partner, died on 28 November, 33 days before his 100th birthday.
why: Buffett later called him the 'architect' of the modern Berkshire. Raised the succession question again; Buffett was 93.

title: Berkshire becomes a trillion-dollar company
what: In August Berkshire Hathaway became the first company outside the technology industry in the United States to be valued at more than one trillion dollars. A single Class A share reached 700,000 dollars. Berkshire has substantially increased its holdings of short-term Treasury bills.
why: The peak of the long climb: 260 dollars a share when the game began. The Treasury-bill detail is from the 2024 letter (published February 2025).

title: Buffett, 94, announces he will step down as chief executive
what: At Berkshire's annual meeting on 3 May Warren Buffett said he would ask the board to make Greg Abel, vice chairman for the non-insurance businesses, chief executive at the end of the year. On 4 May the board voted unanimously to appoint Abel president and chief executive from 1 January 2026; Buffett remains chairman.
why: The end of the Buffett era, 60 years after he took control.

title: Greg Abel takes over Berkshire
what: Greg Abel became Berkshire Hathaway's chief executive on 1 January, with Warren Buffett staying on as chairman. This month Berkshire completed the purchase of the chemicals maker OxyChem from Occidental Petroleum, announced last year.
why: Where the arc stands: the first Berkshire letter not written by Buffett (dated 28 February 2026) reports cash and Treasuries above 370 billion dollars and promises buybacks only below intrinsic value.
